message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This review is grounded in two months of actual till data for every main course, a full competitor price check, and the latest supplier information, so the recommendations are not guesswork. The price increases are modest and targeted: each of the three dishes stays below the midpoint of competitor prices for that dish, so we remain the value option in the area, and with 60% of bookings from repeat guests our customer base is loyal enough to absorb a pound or two. The projected effect is simple to check, £810 a week or about £42,000 a year in additional gross profit, which lifts our main-course margin to about 71%. I also think the menu-mix decision is clear-cut: the data show the mushroom risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so replacing it with a seasonal special is an easy improvement. Monitoring for eight weeks gives us an early warning if volumes move. Overall I believe these changes are sensible, low-risk and well evidenced.
</author>

<document>
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.
</document>
response:
## What the paper proposes

The paper makes two proposals for 1 April:

- **Price rises:** fish and chips +£1, burger +£1, steak +£2, all staying below the midpoint of competitors' prices. Projected gain: £810 a week (£42,120 a year) in gross profit, lifting main-course margin to about 71%.
- **Remove the mushroom risotto** as the weakest-margin, lowest-selling main, replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

I checked these against Table 1 and sections 3–5. The price rises are justified, arguably more strongly than the paper says, because they also need to absorb a beef cost rise. But the projection leaves out that cost rise and probably VAT. The case for removing the risotto is the reverse of what the table shows.

## 1. The risotto has the highest margin on the menu

Table 1 shows the risotto at **80%**, the best of any dish. Its profit per plate (£11.20) is above the curry (£10.90) and burger (£10.80), and it is only joint-lowest on sales, tied with specials at 90 plates. "Weakest margin on the menu" is wrong.

Replacing it carries two risks:

- **Lower profit per plate.** Specials currently run at 64%. A vegetarian special at the same £14 and 64% margin would earn about £8.96 a plate, roughly £200 a week less at 90 plates.
- **Losing whole tables.** The risotto is probably the main vegetarian option. If a group can't find something for its vegetarian, the restaurant can lose the whole booking, not just one plate.

If the real concern is that the risotto doesn't sell well, the options are to rework or reposition it, not to remove it on margin grounds.

## 2. The projection ignores the beef rise

Section 4 says beef rises **12% from 1 April**, the same date as the new prices. Section 5.3 holds food costs flat.

How much this matters depends on what share of each plate's cost is beef. Assuming steak is mostly beef and the burger is about half:

- **Steak:** +about £1.25 a plate × 120 = about £150 a week
- **Burger:** +about £0.25–0.50 a plate × 260 = about £65–£130 a week

That is roughly **£215–£280 a week** of extra cost the projection doesn't include. On steak, most of the £2 rise goes on the beef increase.

## 3. The figures are probably VAT-inclusive

UK menu prices include 20% VAT, and Table 1's margins appear to be calculated on menu price. If so, each £1 price rise brings in about £0.83 of actual revenue, and the true margins are lower than shown. For example, fish and chips is about 63% on the VAT-exclusive price, not 69%.

Confirm how the 70% target is measured.

## 4. Corrected projection

| | Weekly | Annual |
|---|---|---|
| As stated | £810 | £42,120 |
| Excluding VAT | about £675 | about £35,100 |
| Excluding VAT, less the beef rise (estimated) | **about £400–£460** | **about £21,000–£24,000** |

**Main-course margin barely moves.** The paper's 71% holds only if beef costs stay flat. Including the beef rise, margin stays at about 69.5%, essentially unchanged. This uses an estimate for specials' prices, which Table 1 doesn't give.

**This strengthens the case for the rises.** They are largely what's needed to hold margin against the beef increase, not a boost to it. The paper should make that argument directly, and should not promise the owners £42,000.

## 5. Monitoring needs a better baseline

The paper compares April–May sales against January–February. Spring trade is usually busier, and Easter falls on 5 April 2026. Volumes could look like they "held" even if the price rises cost some covers.

Compare instead with **April–May 2025**, adjusting if the two Easters fall differently.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Trading days:** Section 2 says the restaurant opens Wednesday to Sunday, which is five days. Section 8 says "six trading days". Fix one of them.
- **Repeat guests cut both ways.** The 60% repeat rate shows loyalty, but regulars are also the people most likely to notice price rises. The 2024 precedent ("no visible effect on bookings") is useful, but bookings are not plates or spend per head.
- **Weekday lunch trade:** it's called "a small share" but not quantified. Give the figure, since it is the most price-sensitive trade.
- **Overall margin:** the 67% → 70% target covers all courses. Mains alone are unlikely to restore it.

## 7. What holds up

- Table 1's margins and plate counts are correct, with plates totalling 1,050.
- All three new prices are below the competitor midpoints: £17.98, £16.50 and £29.50.
- The beef increase gives a clear, current reason for the rises.

## 8. Settled and open

**Settled by the paper's own figures:**
- The risotto has the highest margin.
- The projection omits the beef rise from the same date.
- Opening days are stated inconsistently.

**Open:**

| Question | What would settle it |
|---|---|
| Beef's share of the burger and steak plate costs | Recipe costings |
| Whether margins and the target are VAT-inclusive | The accounts |
| Volume response to the rises | Weekly sales against April–May 2025 |
| How many diners rely on the risotto as the vegetarian option | Till data on tables ordering it |

## Recommendation

1. **Approve the three price rises.** Restate them as protecting margin against the beef increase, with a projected gain of about £21,000–£24,000 a year net of VAT and beef costs.
2. **Don't approve removing the risotto** on the stated grounds. If anything changes, keep it as the vegetarian staple and trial the seasonal special alongside it.
3. **Change the monitoring baseline** to April–May 2025.
4. **Correct the opening days.**
